cue: Edges are sharp and the middle is soft. Pale colours fade, and the picture moves in a way that follows what moves.

fov.note: a wider group figure for fish and cephalopods

cpd.note: inside the measured range of 0.36 to 12 cycles per degree; the app takes a middle figure

fall.note: the app's own fall with light

dof.note: a slit pupil in bright light gives a deep focus; strength is the app's

sat.note: the app's choice to show no colour, following the colour blindness reports

topoA.note: the app's own sharpness gradient along the long axis

topoS.note: the app's own sharpness gradient across

ripple.note: the app's own ripple that follows movement

sheen.note: the app's choice of no sheen, since no tapetum has been reported

rows: An octopus resolves about 3 to 12 cycles per degree in the best measures, a squid about 0.6 to 6.6, and a cuttlefish about 0.4 to 0.9 in one study. The picture is blurred to a middle figure between these.
Octopus studies find no colour sense in behaviour tests, and most cephalopods have one visual pigment. The picture is therefore greyscale.
The octopus pupil is round in the dark and narrows to a horizontal slit in bright light, so the picture uses a slit.
Coleoid cephalopods see roughly 180 degrees from one side. The squid and cuttlefish records give fields from 117 to 342 degrees, so the picture uses a wide 180 degrees.
The brightness gain, the shallow focus, the soft middle, the faint ripple and the absence of sheen are the app's own settings, set inside the measured limits.
Some settings in this view are the app's own choices, because no measurement gives them. They are set to give a fair picture of the animal and can be tuned by hand.
